posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: Are they temperature stabilized? With MBDCG holography exposure times of more than 10 minutes are often necessary. Also, I have found that a non-temperature stabilized diode laser will slowly allow it's wavelength to drift even when it does not mode hop. This results in significantly less bright holograms. For short exposure times this is not a problem, but for longer exposures it is. I have spent six months trying to find out why my MBDCG's were dim. It turned out to be the slow temperature drift (fixed with TEC controller).

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> Does the laser have to be equipped with this ability from the beginning?In my opinion, yes. Hans has reported excellent results with his design, which is on the Wiki. Years ago, I tried much the same procedure (as far as I can tell) but it didn't work out for some reason. I got better stability with TEC turned off! (And I used a good controller, etc., from Thorlabs.) TEC-cooled laser diodes require a fair amount of work and expense. When it doesn't work out, it's a real disappointment.The biggest problem with homemade TEC lasers is that the temperature sensor needs a good thermal contact with the part of wich the temperature needs to be sensed. Just sticking the sensor against a part of the laser is not sufficient because too much lag will exist between the actual temperature and the measured temperature. Also, it is good to place the sensor very close to the Peltier element. Again to reduce lag (here between commanded temperature and sensed tempere). If these two conditions are not met, the actual laser temperature will swing slightly around the commanded temperature. This causes mode hops and wavelength drifts. In my sensor I drilled a little hole in the base plate, close to the Peltier and placed the sensor in that hole, and filled the hole up with thermally conducting epoxy glue.After you are able to keep the temperature of the laser constant, it is necessary to find the temperature at which the diode does not mode hop. This can be done by inspecting the light when it is reflected from a DVD.A good and stable temperature always improves the quality of the laser light. And I believe it is essential, especially for the beginning holographer, because one (very BIG) variable is eliminated from the holography laboratorium.If you follow my directions on the wikihttp://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... aser_Diode, you will have no problems at all to make a good diode laser.Does the laser have to be equipped with this ability from the beginning?

Not to make a hologram. But if you want to be able to analyze why some holograms are dim, striped, vague, or have little depth, the answer is YES. Temperature stability is essential for a diode laser. Also, while a diode may not be mode hopping before you start your exposure, it might start to do this during your exposure and an expensive plate is wasted. Somehow diodes love to mode hop. When they start, they never stop until you change the current or temperature.

> **wler:** So again, I wonder how the Integraf module is doing 100mW without giving a mess. Perhaps they found a special, better type of diode??

This is a mystery. If it truly is a 650nm diode that does 100mW, and if it's stable enough for 30 second exposures without active temperature control, then it would be worth $245 just for the diode. If it can make holograms without TE cooling, then the chances seem favorable that it can be used for longer exposures, if the diode can be pulled out and used with the system on the Wiki that Hans developed.

As a price comparison, a 635nm 35mW Sanyo diode from Thorlabs costs $384. There is only one 650nm diode, also Sanyo, and it's a low-power one at 7mW. There are some powerful 658nm diodes from Hitachi, Sanyo, and Mitsubishi, including the Hitachi HL6535MG, which is a 90mW diode. They also have a 660nm 130mW Mitsubishi diode, ML101J27.

Maybe it's one of these last two? Maybe Integraf is "approximating" the wavelength as 650nm? That would be aggravating. Maybe they're over-driving the 658nm Hitachi diode, getting it up to 100mW? Or just making a 10nm error in specifying the Mitsubishi diode?

posts.author: wler
posts.content_md:
Or perhaps there is a general rule like that at 50% max power, the diode is better behaved, and they use a 200mW diode (for example)? I don't know the rules of the game, but I would tend to believe that the situation always gets worse the higher you go up in power - high power infrared diodes have sometimes a linewidth of several nanometers, for example, which would be disastrous. 

On top of that, the lack of temp stabilization of that module.... according to what has been found, even at low powers you may have lots of instabilities and chaotic mode hops if you sit on the wrong operating point. It seems one needs to keep the temperature constant to 0.1-0.5 degrees just to stay in a stable region, and drifting out from there may land you in an unstable zone with mode chaos. What I mean that every time you switch the diode on, it should stabilize within a well defined zone of less than a degree spread even to start with. The temperature drift during exposure time must then be of course much less than that at any rate. 

So I really wonder how a non-stabilized module of that power could work reliably. But a true laser specialist may have an answer for this?

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I have found that the best test is still to make a hologram. But to make sure that you are in a region where you suspect no mode hopping, it is wise to do the DVD test first: Adjust the power until you see a mode hop, then adjust the power further until you see the next mode hop. Then put the power in-between those two spots. Interestingly, at some power/temperature settings a diode is multimode, even in-between the mode hopping powers. But if you then choose the next higher (or lower) region between mode hopping power levels, most often at that power setting the diode does not mode hop I have found. (I use a HL6512MG 50mW diode).

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Not having seen the Integraf module, I don't know what it's like. I'guessing it's a diode mounted in a typical cylindrical housing with a collimating lens.

For use with TE cooling, it would be probably be preferable to work with the diode itself (i.e., removed from the housing), as Hans and Colin suggested. If you tried to use the existing housing as part of a TE cooled system, there would be more thermal resistance between the TE cooler and diode (i.e., the imperfect contact between the exterior of the housing and the metal cooling plate which is attached to the TEC). This gap could be filled by thermal epoxy, but even though this material is designed to transfer heat, it does so quite poorly. 

So if you were working with the bare diode, the thermal transition might be like this: TEC, thermal epoxy, cold plate, thermal grease, diode.

If you tried to use the existing housing/diode, it might be: TEC, thermal epoxy, cold plate, thermal epoxy, diode housing, thermal grease, diode.

The housing would just add more complexity, and this would hold true for the thermistor placement as well.

Colin, were you thinking of a specific 150mW diode?
